1.title: Cluster Architecture and Extension Interfaces
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Cluster Architecture and Extension Interfaces. It covers the exam area Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Understand extension interfaces (C N I, C S I (Container Storage Interface), C R I (Container Runtime Interface), and so on). This module also gives the map you need for every troubleshooting task. Practice with seven hands-on labs worth twenty-eight points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration (twenty-five percent). Practice in this module: seven labs, twenty-eight points, about twenty-eight minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero (kubeadm-style layout in kind nodes).

1.title: The map of a cluster
1.text: The map of a cluster. The figure shows this: Control plane and worker node components.

1.title: The map of a cluster, continued
1.text: The map of a cluster. A cluster has a control plane (the decision makers) and worker nodes (where Pods run). In a kubeadm-style cluster the control plane runs as static Pods on the control plane node.

1.title: The map of a cluster, continued
1.text: The map of a cluster. kube A P I server. Where it runs: control plane, static Pod. Job: The front door. Every kube control call, every kubelet and controller talks to it. Only it talks to E T C D. E T C D. Where it runs: control plane, static Pod. Job: The database of all cluster state. kube scheduler. Where it runs: control plane, static Pod. Job: Picks a node for each new Pod. kube controller manager. Where it runs: control plane, static Pod. Job: Runs the controllers (Deployment, Replica Set, Node, Namespace,...) that move actual state toward desired state.

1.title: The map of a cluster, continued
1.text: The map of a cluster. kubelet. Where it runs: every node, a systemd service (not a Pod). Job: Starts the containers of Pods assigned to its node and reports status. kube proxy. Where it runs: every node, Daemon Set. Job: Programs Service rules on the node. Container runtime. Where it runs: every node. Job: Runs containers (here container D ). Core D N S. Where it runs: Deployment in kube system. Job: Cluster D N S. Exam fact to remember: the kubelet is a service on the node. If it stops, the node goes Not Ready. The other control plane parts are Pods, so you read their logs with kube control logs or, when the A P I server is down, with C R I C T L.

1.title: Static Pods
1.text: Static Pods. A static Pod is defined by a file on a node, not by the A P I server. The kubelet watches a directory and runs whatever manifest it finds there. The A P I server shows a read-only mirror Pod whose name ends with the node name ( E T C D C K A control plane ). Directory: set by static Pod Path in the kubelet config file slash var slash lib slash kubelet slash config dot yaml. On kube A D M clusters it is slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests. Create one: write a Pod manifest into that directory on that node. Remove it by deleting the file. kube control delete pod only removes the mirror, and the kubelet recreates it. Exam tip: The control plane runs as static Pods: to change one, edit its manifest in slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests and the kubelet restarts it.

1.title: Static Pods, continued
1.text: Static Pods. Edit a control plane component (for example an A P I server flag) by editing its manifest. The kubelet restarts it by itself. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Static Pods, continued
1.text: Static Pods. The mirror Pod appears as static web- node name; its owner reference kind is Node.

1.title: Where things live (kubeadm layout)
1.text: Where things live (kube A D M layout). Static Pod manifests. slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests or. Certificates. slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash pki or (E T C D's in slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash pki slash E T C D or ). Admin kube config. slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash admin dot conf. Kubelet configuration. slash var slash lib slash kubelet slash config dot yaml. C N I (Container Network Interface) configuration. slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d or. Service Cluster I P range. the service cluster ip range flag flag in kube A P I server dot yaml. Find an A P I server flag fast. Exam tip: Remember three paths: manifests in slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests, certificates in slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash pki, C N I configuration in slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d.

1.title: Where things live (kubeadm layout), continued
1.text: Where things live (kube A D M layout). The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Container runtime and crictl
1.text: Container runtime and C R I C T L. The kubelet talks to the runtime through the Container Runtime Interface (C R I). Here the runtime is container D. C R I C T L is the node-level tool that speaks C R I, and it is your tool when kube control does not work. List running containers. C R I C T L ps (add dash a for stopped ones). Filter by name. C R I C T L ps the name flag kube proxy. I D s only. C R I C T L ps the name flag kube proxy dash q. Logs of a container. C R I C T L logs id. List Pod sandboxes. C R I C T L pods. Exam tip: When the A P I server is down, kube control cannot help: use C R I C T L ps and C R I C T L logs on the node.

1.title: Extension interfaces: CNI, CSI, CRI
1.text: Extension interfaces: C N I, C S I, C R I. Kubernetes does not ship networking, storage or a runtime. It defines interfaces and plugins implement them. C R I. Full name: Container Runtime Interface. What plugs in: the runtime (container D, C R I-O). How you see it: kube control get nodes dash o wide (C O N T A I N E R-R U N T I M E column). C N I. Full name: Container Network Interface. What plugs in: the Pod network (kind net, Calico, Cilium,...). How you see it: config file in slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d or on the node. C S I. Full name: Container Storage Interface. What plugs in: storage drivers. How you see it: kube control get csidrivers, kube control get storageclass. Exam tip: Remember the three plug-in interfaces by what they plug in: C R I is the runtime, C N I is the network, C S I is the storage.

1.title: Extension interfaces: CNI, CSI, CRI, continued
1.text: Extension interfaces: C N I, C S I, C R I. No C N I plugin means Pods stay Container Creating and nodes are Not Ready. In the lab cluster the C N I is kind net; its file is slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d slash ten kind net dot conflist. A Runtime Class chooses a runtime handler for a Pod. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Extension interfaces: CNI, CSI, CRI, continued
1.text: Extension interfaces: C N I, C S I, C R I. If the handler does not exist in container D, the Pod never starts (see Lab one point five's wrong answer).

1.title: How a Pod gets created (the story)
1.text: How a Pod gets created (the story). The figure shows this: How a Pod gets created.

1.title: How a Pod gets created (the story), continued
1.text: How a Pod gets created (the story). kube control sends the request to the A P I server, which authenticates, authorizes, validates and writes it to E T C D. The Deployment controller (in the controller manager) creates a Replica Set, which creates Pods. The scheduler sees Pods with no node and writes a node name. The kubelet on that node sees its Pod, asks the runtime (C R I) to start containers and the C N I plugin to wire the network. kube proxy keeps Service rules current on every node. Exam use: when a Pod is stuck, find which step stopped. Pending with no node equals scheduler. Container Creating for long equals C N I, image pull or volume. Not Ready node equals kubelet.

1.title: Lab 1.1: service cidr
1.text: Lab one point one: service cidr. This task is worth three points, and you should plan about three minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Find the I P range from which Service Cluster I P s are allocated in this cluster and write it (for example ten dot zero dot zero dot zero slash eight ) to about slash answers slash svc cidr dot txt. Hint: it is a flag of one control plane component. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 1.1: service cidr, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run S S H C K A control plane grep service cluster ip range slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests slash kube A P I server dot yaml. Then S S H C K A control plane grep dash o service cluster ip range zero to nine. or slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests slash kube A P I server dot, and so on. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.2: static pod
2.text: Lab one point two: static pod. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Create a static Pod named static web with image engine X alpine on the node C K A worker. Find the directory the kubelet watches for static Pod manifests from the kubelet configuration file. The Pod must run in the default namespace. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.2: static pod, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run S S H C K A worker grep static Pod Path slash var slash lib slash kubelet slash config dot yaml. S S H C K A worker mkdir dash p slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests cat slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests slash static web dot yaml. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.3: crictl container
2.text: Lab one point three: C R I C T L container. This task is worth four points, and you should plan about four minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. On the node C K A worker, use C R I C T L to find the I D of the running container named kube proxy and write the full container I D to about slash answers slash cid dot txt on the host. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.3: crictl container, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run S S H C K A worker C R I C T L ps the name flag kube proxy dash q about slash answers slash cid dot txt. Then cat about slash answers slash cid dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.4: cni config
2.text: Lab one point four: cni config. This task is worth three points, and you should plan about three minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Pod networking on node C K A worker is set up by a C N I plugin. Find the name of the C N I configuration file in the directory the kubelet runtime reads ( slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d ) on that node and write only the file name to about slash answers slash cni dot txt. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.4: cni config, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run S S H C K A worker ls slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d about slash answers slash cni dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.5: runtimeclass
2.text: Lab one point five: runtimeclass. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Create a Runtime Class named standard that uses the container runtime handler runc. Then create a Pod named rtc in the namespace rt with image engine X alpine that uses this Runtime Class. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.5: runtimeclass, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.5: runtimeclass, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab one point five: runtimeclass, Solution, continued. kube control dash n rt apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n rt wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash rtc the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds.

2.title: Lab 1.6: node versions
2.text: Lab one point six: node versions. This task is worth four points, and you should plan about four minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Write one line per node to about slash answers slash versions dot txt on the host, in the form node name kubelet version (for example node one version one dot thirty-seven dot zero ), sorted by node name, using Jason Path or custom columns (no header line). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.6: node versions, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control get nodes dash o json path range dot items dot metadata dot name dot status dot node Info dot kubelet Version newline end sort about slash answers slash versions dot txt. Then cat about slash answers slash versions dot txt. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 1.7: etcd image
2.text: Lab one point seven: E T C D image. This task is worth four points, and you should plan about four minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. Find the container image (name and tag) that the E T C D static Pod uses, by reading the manifest on the control plane node (not by asking the A P I server), and write only the image to about slash answers slash E T C D image dot txt on the host. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 1.7: etcd image, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run S S H C K A control plane grep image slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests slash E T C D dot yaml. Then S S H C K A control plane grep image slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests slash E T C D dot yaml awk print two about slash answers slash E T, and so on. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which component is the only one that talks to E T C D? Answer: The A P I server. Question two. How does the kubelet run on a kube A D M cluster node? Answer: As a systemd service, not as a Pod. Question three. Where do static Pod manifests live, and how do you find the exact path? Answer: Usually slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests; the static Pod Path field in slash var slash lib slash kubelet slash config dot yaml gives the path.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. You run kube control delete pod on a static Pod. What happens? Answer: Only the mirror Pod is removed; the kubelet recreates it. Delete the manifest file to remove the Pod. Question five. Which tool inspects containers on a node when the A P I server is down? Answer: C R I C T L. Question six. What do C N I, C S I and C R I each plug in? Answer: C N I the Pod network, C S I storage drivers, C R I the container runtime.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. A new node stays Not Ready and Pods stay Container Creating. Which extension is the first suspect? Answer: The C N I plugin (its configuration in slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d or ). Question eight. Where is the Service Cluster I P range configured? Answer: The the service cluster ip range flag flag of the A P I server (its static Pod manifest).

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Control plane: A P I server, E T C D, scheduler, controller-manager as static Pods. Node: kubelet (systemd), kube proxy (Daemon Set), runtime. Static Pod dir: static Pod Path in slash var slash lib slash kubelet slash config dot yaml, usually slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash manifests. Certificates: slash E T C slash Kubernetes slash pki or. C N I config: slash E T C slash cni slash net dot d or. Node-level container tool: C R I C T L ps, C R I C T L logs. Interfaces: C R I runtime, C N I network, C S I storage. In the next module, we continue the course.
